titre: The Tablet That Changed How the Flood Is Read
accroche: In December 1872, a self-taught engraver's apprentice announces that he has read, on an Assyrian tablet, an account of a flood almost identical to that of Genesis.
contenu_vulgarise:
On December 3, 1872, before the Society of Biblical Archaeology in London, a 32-year-old man presents the translation of a clay tablet covered in cuneiform: an account of a flood, with a boat, animals taken aboard in pairs, birds released to look for dry land. The audience, used to reading Genesis as a text without precedent, understands at once what this implies. The man's name is George Smith. He never attended university: an engraver's apprentice at 14, he taught himself cuneiform, alone, during his lunch breaks, at the British Museum.

## An Assyrian Tablet, a Much Older Story

The tablet Smith has just read, now catalogued as K.3375 at the British Museum, is the eleventh of a long Babylonian poem, the Epic of Gilgamesh. It was copied in the 7th century BCE at Nineveh, in the library of King Ashurbanipal, but the story it carries is much older: it belongs to a Mesopotamian flood tradition attested since the beginning of the 2nd millennium BCE, in which the hero Utnapishtim builds a boat on the order of a god to escape a flood decreed by the others.

The resemblance to Genesis (the ark, the pairs of animals, the bird sent out to reconnoiter, the boat that comes to rest on a mountain) is too precise to be chance. It does not prove, however, that the Bible “copied” Gilgamesh: both texts more likely draw on a stock of still older Mesopotamian stories, shared throughout the region, of which the biblical version would be a late rewriting, offering its own theological meaning to a story that no one in the ancient Near East would have found original in itself.

The public success of Smith's announcement is immediate. The daily newspaper the *Daily Telegraph* finances, to the tune of a thousand guineas, an expedition back to Nineveh to look for the missing fragments of the story. In barely a few weeks, against all expectation, Smith finds them.

## What This Changes

The significance of the discovery goes beyond mere archaeological curiosity. For centuries, the flood story could be read as an event without equivalent, affecting all of humanity without any other tradition having kept its memory. Tablet K.3375 changes this reading without settling the theological question of its truth: it shows that the story of a destructive flood followed by a rescue by boat was already circulating, under other names and for other gods, well before Genesis was put in writing. What the Bible tells is no longer isolated: it is one voice, recognizable and singular in what it does with the story, within a regional conversation much older than itself.

Smith himself would not have long to explore the aftermath of his discovery: he died of dysentery in 1876, in Aleppo, during a third expedition to the sites that had made his career.

repere.texte: Tablet K.3375, copied in the 7th century BCE at Nineveh, preserves the eleventh part of the Epic of Gilgamesh. Its decipherment, announced on December 3, 1872, before the Society of Biblical Archaeology in London, was followed by a subscription of a thousand guineas from the Daily Telegraph to fund a new expedition to Nineveh.
repere.source: The British Museum, online collection; George Smith (Assyriologist), Wikipedia

carte.punch: A self-taught engraver's apprentice read the real flood in 1872: a Mesopotamian one.
carte.idee: In December 1872, George Smith deciphers on an Assyrian tablet an account of a flood almost identical to that of Genesis. The discovery places the biblical story within a much older Mesopotamian tradition widely shared across the region.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Overview of the flood story in the Epic of Gilgamesh and its Mesopotamian and biblical parallels.

quiz.question: What does George Smith's discovery of the flood tablet in 1872 show?
choix: That the flood story of Genesis belongs to an older, shared Mesopotamian tradition
That Genesis copied the Epic of Gilgamesh word for word
That the biblical flood took place exactly in the 7th century BCE
That the Epic of Gilgamesh was written after Genesis in order to contradict it
quiz.explication: The tablet, copied in the 7th century BCE, preserves a much older version of the story, common to several Mesopotamian traditions: it places Genesis within a shared regional stock rather than in isolation, without however establishing direct copying or dating the event itself, and without any text preceding the other in the reverse direction.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What training did George Smith have before deciphering the flood tablet?
choix: He studied Assyriology at the University of Oxford
He was trained by a British missionary at Nineveh
He had no university training: an engraver's apprentice, he taught himself cuneiform at the British Museum
He took the courses of a French epigrapher in Paris
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Smith never attended university: an engraver's apprentice at 14, he taught himself cuneiform, alone, during his lunch breaks, at the British Museum.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does tablet K.3375 come from, and when was it copied?
choix: From Babylon, copied in the 2nd millennium BCE
From Nineveh, copied in the 7th century BCE in the library of King Ashurbanipal
From Susa, copied in the 4th century BCE under the Achaemenids
From Ur, copied in the 3rd millennium BCE
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Tablet K.3375 was copied in the 7th century BCE at Nineveh, in the library of King Ashurbanipal, even though the story it carries goes back to a much older tradition.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does George Smith die, in 1876?
choix: Of dysentery, in Aleppo, during a third expedition to the sites that had made his career
Drowned in the wreck of the ship bringing him back to London
Of old age, after retiring from the British Museum
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Smith dies of dysentery in Aleppo in 1876, during a third expedition to the Mesopotamian sites that had made his career as an Assyriologist.
